svg.title: Medicines & antibodies
svg.desc: Antibiotics & symptoms: Antibiotics such as penicillin treat bacteria; choose an effective one. Resistance makes infections harder to treat. Antibiotics do not kill viruses. Viruses reproduce inside cells, making safe targeting difficult. Painkillers relieve symptoms without killing pathogens. Drug origins: Digitalis ← foxglove. Aspirin ← willow. Penicillin: Fleming’s discovery from Penicillium mould. Most new drugs are synthesised; natural chemicals may provide starting points. Testing sequence: Check toxicity, efficacy and dose. Preclinical: cells, tissues, live animals. Clinical: low doses in healthy volunteers, then patients to test effectiveness and optimum dose. Results undergo peer review before publication. Fair comparisons: Placebo: no active drug. Double-blind: patients and assessors do not know allocations. Random allocation, comparable groups and large samples reduce misleading effects. Compare recovery rates and side effects, not raw counts alone. Make monoclonal antibodies: Antigen stimulates mouse lymphocytes. Fuse an antibody-producing lymphocyte with a tumour cell → hybridoma. Select and clone one hybridoma; collect/purify antibodies. Clone makes antibodies with one specific binding site. Uses & limits: Specific binding: pregnancy tests, hormone measurement, pathogen detection; fluorescent tags locate molecules. Attach toxic drugs/radioactive substances/growth blockers to target cancer cells. Targeting reduces unwanted damage but side effects and unsuitable targets can limit benefit.
